text:
Two papers analyse amenable (treatable) mortality. The first compares Hungary, Czechoslovakia, Poland, and East Germany with West Germany, England and Wales, the US, and Canada (1950s–1987). All-cause mortality trends diverged around 1970: Western rates declined steadily, Eastern ones stagnated. In ages 0–64 amenable mortality fell more slowly in Eastern Europe, while non-amenable mortality rose from the late 1960s versus substantial Western declines—the principal reason for Eastern Europe's stalled improvement; priorities should be healthier lifestyles and environment, plus better health services.

Scholz examines Lithuania, Hungary, and Romania versus West Germany, 1980/81–1988 and 1992–1997. West German temporary life expectancy (e0–75) rose 2.7 years (men) and 1.6 (women); Hungarian women gained 1.3; Romanian men lost 1.3. Falling infant mortality, largely amenable conditions, contributed substantially.
